comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: If I am right, the Polynesian adventure began about 5,000 years ago when the inhabitants of Taiwan began putting out to sea into the vast Pacific, mastering extraordinary navigation achievements. The Hawaiians, Maoris, Malagasys, Micro- and Macronesians and many others are their descendants. The Marshal Islanders too are their descendants. In the modern era contact with powerful nations has not been kind to them. The callous trampling of their rights by the US atomic testers is shocking and atrocious. Today climatic warming is going on apace despite more than a century of very clear warnings. The current US president is obscessed with oil and pays companies NOT to build wind farms and solar parks. Ergo: in my opinion the seas will continue to rise and become warmer and more acidic reducing the coral's ability to lay down calcium carbonate. Offhand I have no new suggestions to solve this dilemma. I have a cousin, now deceased, who was a British Colonial Administrator in the Gilbert and Ellice Islands before WWII and spoke fluent Polynesian. He said the people there were beautiful and wonderfully hospitable. When WWII broke out, he remained and went into hiding, serving as a Scout. He passed information on about the movements of Japanese ships, which trusted Polynesians had told him. Most of the Scouts were captured by the Japanese and brutally executed. Your video has inspired me to think much more deeply about the complex webs of cause and effect which the Marshal Islanders are dealing with. Thank you.

comments.author: @TravelBeyond4K
comments.text: Eating freshly caught reef fish and roasted breadfruit right by the lagoon really highlights the raw, self-sustaining lifestyle of the Marshallese. Imports might be expensive, but their traditional food reliance on the land and ocean remains strong. You can taste the genuine coastal simplicity in every meal.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: Thank you - that self-sufficiency really does come through in every part of daily life there.

comments.author: @AmazingDiscoveriesTopUS
comments.text: Ifyour homeland was slowly disappearing beneath the ocean, would you stay and fight for it - or leave and start over somewhere else?

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That's the impossible question so many Pacific island nations are actually facing right now, not hypothetically. Hard to say which choice is braver.
